damp-proofing: Damp in {town} homes usually has one of three causes: condensation from cooking, drying and poor ventilation; penetrating damp through defective pointing, render, gutters or flashings; or rising damp where a damp-proof course has failed or been bridged by raised ground or a patio. The treatment is different for each, which is why we survey before quoting. Injecting a chemical course into a wall that is wet from a leaking gutter wastes money and the wall stays wet.

A survey for {kw} records moisture readings at several heights, checks external ground levels, gutters and downpipes, and looks at ventilation in kitchens and bathrooms. The written report says what we found, what we recommend and what each item costs, so you can fix the cause first and the finish after. Replastering is done once the wall has dried enough, using a lime or salt-resistant plaster where the wall needs it.
rendering: Render on {town} houses ranges from traditional sand and cement to monocouche, silicone and acrylic thin-coat systems over insulation boards. Each needs a different substrate preparation, base coat and curing time, and the right choice depends on the wall, its exposure and whether the building is in a conservation area. Before quoting {kw} we check for hollow areas, cracks at openings, the condition of beads and whether old paint or render must come off.

Weather matters. Render cannot go on in frost, heavy rain or strong sun, so we book external work with a weather margin and tell you if a day has to move. Scaffolding, protection of windows and paths, and removal of waste are listed separately in the written quote. Afterwards you get a note of the system used and its maintenance needs, which is useful when you sell or when an insurer asks.
heating: Heating work in {town} covers boiler servicing and repair, radiator and valve changes, power flushing, controls upgrades and system balancing. Gas work is carried out by Gas Safe registered engineers. Before quoting {kw} we ask for the boiler make and model, the number of radiators, whether the system is open-vented or sealed, and what is going wrong, because cold radiators, noisy pipes and rising bills all have different causes.

A badly balanced system wastes energy: radiators near the boiler run hot while the far rooms stay cold. Balancing sets each lockshield valve so the flow is shared, and a magnetic filter and inhibitor protect the system after a flush. You get a written note of what was done and any readings taken, and we flag parts that are near the end of their life rather than replacing them without asking.
building-surveys: A building survey in {town} looks at the structure, roof, walls, damp, timbers, windows and services of a property, and reports on defects, their likely cause and what to do next. It is not a valuation. Before quoting {kw} we ask about the property's age, construction, size and whether it has been extended or converted, because a Victorian terrace with a cellar needs a different inspection from a 1990s semi.

The report is written in plain English with photos, separating urgent repairs from routine maintenance, and it says where a specialist such as a structural engineer, drainage contractor or electrician should look further. It helps with negotiating a purchase price, planning works after you buy, or setting a maintenance budget for a rented portfolio. We aim to send it within a few working days of the inspection.
plumbing: Plumbing jobs in {town} range from leaks, blocked wastes and dripping taps to new bathroom and kitchen supplies, appliance connections and commercial washrooms. For {kw} we ask what is installed, where the stopcock is, whether the property is a house, flat or commercial unit, and whether there is visible damage below the leak. In flats, a leak can come from the flat above, so we check before opening walls.

We isolate and make safe first, then repair or replace with matching fittings. Where pipework is old lead or corroded steel, we say so and quote replacement separately rather than patching. Commercial jobs are booked around trading hours where possible. You get a written record of the work, and for appliance connections we check for leaks under load before leaving.
joinery: Joinery in {town} covers doors and frames, skirting and architrave, stairs and handrails, built-in storage, windows and repairs to timber that has suffered damp or rot. For {kw} we ask for measurements and photos so we can tell whether a part can be repaired, matched from stock or has to be made. Older houses rarely have standard sizes, and matching period mouldings takes time.

Fire doors are a separate job: a replacement fire door has to be a certified door set with matching frame, intumescent seals, hinges and closer, fitted to the manufacturer's tolerances. We do not swap a fire door leaf into an old frame. Every job gets a written quote listing materials, finishes and making good, and waste is removed when we finish.
plastering: Plastering in {town} includes skimming over existing walls and ceilings, patch repairs after electrical or plumbing work, replastering after damp treatment, and dry lining with plasterboard. For {kw} the area, the condition of the background and whether old plaster must be hacked off decide the price. Blown or cracked plaster over a large area usually needs replacing rather than skimming.

Lime plaster suits older solid-wall buildings because it lets the wall breathe, while gypsum suits modern blockwork and plasterboard. After plastering, new walls need time to dry before painting, typically a week or more depending on thickness and ventilation, and we tell you when it is safe to decorate. Floors and furniture are protected and waste removed.
electrical: Electrical work in {town} includes EICRs, consumer unit changes, rewires, additional circuits, lighting and fault finding. Work is carried out to BS 7671 and notifiable work is certified. For {kw} we ask about the age of the installation, the consumer unit and any recent problems such as tripping, so the engineer arrives with the right test kit and parts.

If testing finds faults, each is coded on the report: C1 danger present, C2 potentially dangerous, C3 improvement recommended, FI further investigation. We quote remedials line by line so you can approve them separately. Certificates and reports are emailed after the visit and we keep a copy so a replacement can be issued if yours goes missing.
kitchen-fire-suppression: Commercial kitchens in {town} with fryers, ranges and woks need a suppression system over the cooking line that discharges a wet chemical agent and cuts the fuel supply if a fire starts in the canopy or ducting. For {kw} we ask for the canopy length, the appliances underneath and the system make, because nozzle layout and agent quantity depend on the appliances.

Systems are serviced at least every six months, with nozzle caps, links, cylinder pressure and the gas shut-off checked and recorded. Changing the appliance line-up, such as swapping a range for a fryer, can mean the system no longer covers the hazard, so tell us before the change. Insurers usually ask for the service certificate, which we email after each visit.
commercial-fit-out: Commercial fit-out in {town} covers shops, offices, cafes and clinics: partitions, ceilings, flooring, lighting and power, washrooms and the fire safety items that go with a new layout. For {kw} we ask for floor plans, the landlord's requirements and the opening date, because landlord consent, building control and the fire strategy can set the programme.

A new layout can change escape routes, emergency lighting and alarm coverage, so we check these as part of the scope rather than leaving them to the end. The written quote breaks the work into packages with a programme, and we coordinate trades so the unit is handed over with certificates for the electrics, alarm and emergency lighting.
landscaping: Landscaping in {town} includes patios, paths, driveways, fencing, turfing, planting and drainage for gardens and communal grounds. For {kw} we ask for rough measurements, photos and how the space is used, because a patio for a family garden and a hard-standing for bins at a block of flats need different bases and falls.

Drainage is the part most often missed: new hard surfaces need to fall away from buildings and drain to a suitable outlet or soakaway, and permeable paving may be needed for front gardens. The written quote lists excavation, sub-base, materials and waste removal, and we tell you how long new turf or planting needs before it is used.
dry-risers: Dry risers in {town} buildings are empty pipes that the fire service charges with water from an inlet at ground level, with landing valves on each floor. For {kw} we ask for the number of floors and outlets and the date of the last test, because risers need a six-monthly visual inspection and an annual wet pressure test under BS 9990.

The annual test pressurises the riser to check for leaks and that valves, inlets and drain valves work. Common faults are missing landing valve straps, seized valves and damaged inlet boxes. Defects are listed on the report with a written quote, and the certificate is emailed to the responsible person after the visit.
emergency-lighting: Emergency lighting in {town} buildings must light escape routes, exits and safety signs if the mains fails. For {kw} we ask for the number of fittings, whether they are self-contained or central battery, and when the last annual duration test was done. BS 5266 expects a monthly function test and an annual full-duration test.

The annual test runs every fitting for its rated duration, usually three hours, and records any that fail early. Failed batteries and lamps are quoted for replacement, and changes to the building layout may need new fittings. The logbook and certificate are updated and emailed, ready for a fire risk assessor or insurer.
insulation: Insulation in {town} homes covers lofts, cavity walls, internal and external solid-wall insulation and floors. For {kw} we ask about the wall type, the age of the property and any damp, because insulation installed over a damp wall or blocking ventilation causes more problems than it solves.

Loft insulation needs ventilation at the eaves and boarded walkways if the loft is used for storage. Solid-wall insulation needs detailing around windows and junctions to avoid cold bridges. The written quote states the material, thickness and expected U-value improvement, and we explain any grant schemes that may apply.
fire-risk-assessments: A fire risk assessment in {town} identifies fire hazards, people at risk and the measures in place, and sets out actions to reduce the risk. For {kw} we ask about the building's use, size, number of storeys and occupants, and whether there is an existing assessment. Our guide price is from £350 for a typical 6-bed HMO in the North West; other properties are POA.

The report records what was found during the walk-round, including fire doors, compartmentation, detection, emergency lighting and escape routes, and lists actions by priority. The responsible person must keep the assessment under review, especially after building work or a change of use. We email the report and can quote the follow-on works separately.
extensions: House extensions in {town} range from single-storey rear kitchens to two-storey side extensions and wraparounds. For {kw} we ask for drawings if you have them, or a sketch with measurements, and whether planning permission or permitted development applies. Building regulations approval is needed for structure, insulation, drainage, electrics and fire safety.

The written quote separates foundations, structure, roof, windows, services and finishes so you can see where the money goes, and lists items excluded such as kitchen units or flooring. We agree a programme, keep the building control officer informed at inspection stages, and hand over completion certificates at the end.
cctv: CCTV in {town} covers homes, shops, offices and blocks of flats, from a few cameras on a recorder to networked systems with remote viewing. For {kw} we ask what you need to see, whether at night, and who will view the footage, because camera position, lens and lighting decide whether a face or number plate is usable.

Systems that record public areas or staff must follow data protection rules: signage, a retention period and a clear purpose. We set up recording schedules, user accounts and remote access, and show you how to export footage. Faults and upgrades are quoted in writing, and we keep a record of the installed equipment for future service visits.
fire-compartmentation: Fire compartmentation in {town} buildings keeps fire and smoke in the area where it starts long enough for people to escape. For {kw} we ask about the building type and any fire risk assessment actions, because surveys often find gaps around pipes, cables and ducts where services pass through fire-resisting walls and floors.

Fire stopping must use tested products installed to the manufacturer's details for the size and type of penetration. We photograph and label each seal so the work can be checked later, and the record forms part of the building's fire safety information. Where a wall or ceiling itself is not fire-resisting, we say so and quote the fix separately.
loft-conversions: Loft conversions in {town} include dormers, hip-to-gable and Velux conversions. For {kw} we check head height, roof structure and the stair position first, because these decide whether a conversion is practical. Most need building regulations approval for structure, insulation, fire safety and the stair, and some need planning permission.

Fire safety is central: a new storey changes the escape route, so the stair is usually protected with fire doors and the house gets mains-wired interlinked smoke alarms. The written quote lists structure, windows, insulation, electrics, plumbing and finishes, and we hand over the completion certificate and electrical certificate at the end.
building-maintenance: Building maintenance in {town} covers reactive repairs and planned work for landlords, managing agents and businesses: gutters, roofs, doors, decoration, small electrical and plumbing jobs and the compliance checks that go with them. For {kw} we ask for a list of buildings, the type of work and how quickly jobs need to be attended.

Planned maintenance saves money: gutters cleared before winter and small roof repairs done in good time stop water getting in. We agree response times, report each job with photos and a written note, and quote anything outside the agreed scope before starting. A shared log keeps compliance dates in one place.
roofing: Roofing work in {town} covers slipped and broken tiles, ridge and verge repairs, flashings, flat roof replacement, gutters and chimney work. For {kw} we ask for photos from the ground and from inside the loft, because water stains inside often appear some distance from where the leak starts.

Safe access is part of the price: some repairs can be done from a ladder or roof ladder, others need scaffolding or a tower. We explain which and why. Flat roofs are quoted by system, such as EPDM, GRP or felt, with the expected life of each. You get photos of the repair and a written note of the work.
